questions.q: Before the Quantitative Revolution, geography was mostly...
options: a descriptive field documenting what places were like and how they differed
concerned with general laws of space
questions.why: For most of its history geography described places. The Quantitative Revolution of the 1950s and 1960s pushed it to be more scientific and mathematical.

options: the physical environment, especially climate, directly determines human behavior, culture and development
near things are more related than distant things
questions.why: Semple and Huntington used it to rank societies by climate. It justified racist hierarchies and colonial rule and was discredited by the mid-20th century.

questions.q: In regional geography (chorology), the goal was to...
options: find general laws that hold everywhere
describe and synthesize the unique character of individual regions
questions.why: Hartshorne's The Nature of Geography (1939) framed geography as the study of areal differentiation, so general laws weren't the goal.

questions.q: What was the main criticism of regional geography?
options: It didn't produce knowledge that could be generalized or tested
questions.why: Its descriptions were rich, but critics said they couldn't be generalized beyond the region or tested.

questions.q: Fred K. Schaefer's 1953 article "Exceptionalism in Geography" argued that geography should...
options: be a science like any other, aimed at discovering general laws of spatial arrangement
questions.why: Schaefer rejected the idea that geography was an "exceptional" discipline that could only describe unique places.

questions.q: Positivism, which the Quantitative Revolution borrowed from, holds that knowledge should be built through...
options: observation, measurement and the testing of hypotheses
questions.why: In practice this meant hypothesis testing, generalization, models and theory, and quantification.

questions.q: How did World War II help bring about the Quantitative Revolution?
options: Geographers worked on applied problems for the government and met operations research, and postwar science funding and the GI Bill expanded research
It made regional geography more popular
questions.why: OSS work pushed geographers toward applied, mathematical problem solving, and the NSF (1950) and the GI Bill fueled the shift after the war.

questions.q: Which university is usually considered the center of the Quantitative Revolution in the late 1950s?
questions.why: William Garrison's students at Washington, the "space cadets," included Berry, Bunge, Morrill, Marble, Nystuen, Dacey and Tobler. The other three were also important centers.

questions.q: Von Thünen's model predicts that perishable, heavy goods like dairy are produced...
questions.why: Transport cost drives the concentric rings, so goods that spoil or are expensive to move are produced near the market.

questions.q: Gravity models propose that interaction between two places is...
options: proportional to the size of the places and inversely proportional to the distance between them
questions.why: The idea borrows from Newton. Ravenstein had already noticed in the 1880s that most migrants travel short distances.

questions.q: Why does the reading say Hägerstrand's spatial diffusion work matters for this course?
options: It was one of the first uses of simulation (Monte Carlo methods) in geography
questions.why: You'll use Monte Carlo simulation later in the course, for example to test point patterns against randomness.

questions.q: Which assumption did the early spatial models share?
options: A flat, uniform landscape (an isotropic plain), rational cost-minimizing decision makers and perfect information
questions.why: These assumptions made the models mathematically tractable, and they became the main target of later critiques.

questions.q: Humanistic geographers like Yi-Fu Tuan argued that the Quantitative Revolution...
options: stripped geography of human experience; people experience places full of meaning, memory and emotion
questions.why: Humanistic geography emphasized qualitative methods and the subjective experience of place.

questions.q: A radical geography critique of a model that explains segregation as the result of individual housing choices would say it...
options: ignores why the pattern exists and who benefits, such as racism, redlining and capitalist land markets
questions.why: Radical geographers like David Harvey asked why patterns exist and who benefits from them, not just what the pattern looks like.

questions.q: Feminist geographers criticized transportation models built around the commute to work because they...
options: ignored complex trip chains like school drop-offs, errands and caregiving that fall disproportionately on women
questions.why: The "rational economic actor" in many models was implicitly a white, middle-class man, and the questions and data reflected that.

options: quantitative methods and critical perspectives can work together, asking who collected the data, what assumptions are built in and who the results serve
questions.why: Mei-Po Kwan's feminist GIS work is the reading's example. Ground Truth (1995) had argued that GIS is not neutral.
